opening.headline: When multiple tool calls are included in a single response, it explains what rules should be used to return the results to avoid confusion.
body: The request “Tell me tomorrow’s schedule and weather” requires two tools: schedule inquiry and weather inquiry. A model can send both calls together in a single response. At this time, if the app only returns the first result or sends results mixed in the order of arrival, the schedule and weather will be reversed or an error will occur.

In this class, we will look at the criteria for distinguishing between parallel and sequential calls, the rules for grouping results by call ID and returning them in one message, and how to return failed calls as errors. Finally, we cover how to design tool responses to be token efficient.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain parallel calls and result return formats
You can distinguish between sequential and parallel calls.

screens.title: Multiple tools must be called at once, but processing the results is complicated.
screens.lead: Read the two failure scenes below. In both scenes, the calls were made correctly, but a problem arose in the step of returning the results.

visual.alt: Illustration showing two calls in one response and two possible paths to incorrect results.
labels: Failure 1: Return only the first result
Failure 2: Return shuffled order of arrival

paragraphs: A user requested, “Tell me your schedule and weather for tomorrow.” The model sent two calls, `get_calendar` and `get_weather`, in one response. Since there are two tools, they must return two results.

This is my first failure. When the app returns only the first result, the model throws an error while waiting for the result of the second call. From the model's perspective, there is no result from either of the two requested calls, so the conversation does not continue.

This is my second failure. Some apps shuffle and send results in the order in which they were finished first, rather than in the order in which they were called. If the weather query is finished first, the weather result comes first, and the model reads this as a schedule result, so the schedule and weather are reversed. The question in this lesson is by what rule should the results be returned?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Even if both the order and number are correct, could the results be distorted? By the end of the class, you will be able to clearly state the criteria that bind calls and results.

screens.outro: First, let's consider a case where multiple tools are needed.

screens.title: Do you ever need multiple tools for a single request?
screens.lead: When you select each case, the instructor's thoughts unfold. First think about whether there has been a similar situation in your app and then press it. You will not enter or submit an answer.

items.prompt: I want to see the schedule and weather together
items.answer: The two queries do not require each other's results. These independent calls are safe to run concurrently and reduce overall time. This is a representative case of parallel calls in this class.

items.prompt: I want to see prices in multiple cities together.
items.answer: This is when the same tool is called multiple times with different arguments for each city. Since they are also independent read operations, they can be executed in parallel. When the same tool is called multiple times, it becomes more important to separate the results by ID.

items.prompt: When the next call can only be made if there is a previous result
items.answer: For example, if you search for a user and then send a message with that user's ID. Since the result of the previous call becomes the input for the next call, they cannot be executed simultaneously and must be continued in order.

items.prompt: How do I distinguish between independent calls and subsequent calls?
items.answer: This can be done by looking at whether the result of one call is the input of another call, or whether the side effects of one call affect the other call. These standards are practiced with examples in demonstrations and application screens.

screens.outro: Let's start by looking at how parallel and sequential calls are represented in each provider.

screens.title: Parallel tool calls and sequential calls
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn how the three providers handle parallel calls and who determines the order of execution.

visual.alt: Illustration comparing the time axis when executing the same two calls in parallel and sequentially.

tabs.label: Claude
tabs.body: Claude can basically contain multiple `tool_use` blocks in one response, where `stop_reason` becomes `tool_use`. The execution order is determined by the app, not the API. You can run them simultaneously, or one by one in the order they appear. If you want to turn off parallel calls, leave `disable_parallel_tool_use` true.

tabs.label: Gemini
tabs.body: Gemini distinguishes between parallel function calls, which call independent functions all at once, and composite function calls, which receive previous results and continue in order. The documentation explains that the model supports both calling multiple functions in one turn and calling them in sequence. This distinction differs in how either app returns results.

tabs.label: OpenAI
tabs.body: OpenAI allows a model to call multiple functions in one turn, and leaving `parallel_tool_calls` false will cause exactly 0 or 1 tool to be called. In models that support it, built-in tools and function calls can be written together in parallel, but built-in tools cannot be included in a bundle of parallel calls.

tabs.label: Judgment of execution order
tabs.body: For either provider, it is the app that determines the execution order. Independent read operations are generally safe to run concurrently. If the side effects of one call affect another, or if the results of an earlier call become input to a later call, they must be executed in order. It is allowed for apps to run sequentially even if they are received in parallel.

screens.outro: Now that we've decided on how to execute, let's read the rules that return the results line by line.

screens.title: Result ID matching: Read calls and results line by line
screens.lead: Select a highlighted passage in the message below to see an explanation of how the call and result pair up. Follow the results of the two calls a1 and b2.

visual.alt: Two tool_use blocks and two tool_result blocks connected by ID.

marks.note: The call identifier created by the model. Even if there are two calls in one response, `stop_reason` is one `tool_use`. Your app must handle both calls and use the same identifier when returning the result.

Result of call with id a1. If this value is misaligned with the call's id, the schedule result will be read as a weather result, and the schedule and weather will be reversed. The id determines the pairing, not the order of the results.

Calls that failed or failed to execute must also return a result to be matched. The failed b2 displays `is_error` as true and writes the reason in content. An error result is returned along with a brief explanation in the same way for calls that were not executed.

In one user message, we put all tool_result blocks before text. If you put text in front, an API format error (400) may occur. Distinguish this from parallel call problems that arise when splitting the result into multiple user messages.

screens.outro: Now that we've paired the results, let's see how to deal with error and response size.

screens.title: Error returns and token-efficient responses
screens.lead: Switch between the two states to see how the same tool's results differ between detailed and concise responses.

states.label: Detailed response
states.body: The detailed response returns all low-level identifiers that the model can use for subsequent operations. In the example from Anthropic's tooling article, this detailed response is 206 tokens long. Low-level identifiers like `uuid`, `mime_type` take up context with little help in the model's next actions. Responses that will take up a lot of context should have default values ​​for pagination, range selection, filters, and truncation, and Claude Code limits tool responses to the default 25,000 tokens.

states.label: concise response
states.body: A concise response returns only high-signal information. In the example from the same article, this response is 72 tokens, or about a third of the detailed response. Placing the `response_format` parameter in the tool, which selects between `concise` and `detailed`, allows the model to choose the level of detail in its response as needed. If the tool fails to run, place `is_error` in Claude's `tool_result` as true to indicate the error, and write the error message as helpful information to guide the next attempt, rather than as cryptic code. For example, “Send date in YYYY-MM-DD format” is much more useful for the model to fix on the next call than “Input error”.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the principle, let’s classify whether each scenario is parallel or sequential.

screens.title: Analysis: Distinguish between sequential and parallel calls
screens.lead: Read the table from top to bottom to follow how the instructor determines whether each scenario is parallel or sequential. It would be a good idea to apply the questions in the Basis for Judgment column to your situation as well.

data.caption: Determination of execution method for each scenario
rows: This is because the two queries are independent read operations that do not require each other's results.
Search for user ID and send message to that ID
This is because the result of the previous call becomes the input for the latter call, so the latter call can only be made when the previous call ends.
Check the weather for two cities
This is because they are independent read operations calling the same tool with different arguments.
This is because there are side effects and order is important, so you need to see whether the previous step was successful before executing the next step.
These are read operations that are independent of each other. This is what Claude's guide does as an example of parallel calls.
data.notes: There are two criteria for judgment. First, check whether the result of one call is the input of another call, and then whether the order is important because of side effects. You must be able to answer no to both questions before you can send them in parallel. If neither, then parallel is safer. It is also possible for the app to execute calls received in parallel sequentially, and if the previous call fails, an error result is returned to the call that was not executed. If the decision is ambiguous, it is safer to execute sequentially, and it is sufficient to obtain speed only from independent read calls.

screens.outro: Now that we have established the classification criteria, we will read and correct the resulting messages that are inconsistent.

screens.title: Explanation: Reading and correcting inconsistent result messages
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to follow the instructor as he corrects the incorrect result messages one by one. There are two calls: a1 and b2.

steps.title: Stage 1 situation
steps.body: The app requested `get_calendar` and `get_weather`, and the model sent two blocks of `tool_use` with ids a1 and b2 in one response. The app ran both simultaneously and the schedule was a success and the weather was a failure.

steps.title: Step 2 Read the problem message
steps.body: The `content` of the user message sent by the app is only `[{text: "This is the result"}, {tool_result, tool_use_id: a1}]`. `text` in the first line precedes `tool_result`, and there is no result for b2 at all.

steps.title: Step 3 Find the cause
steps.body: There are two causes: First, `tool_result` must be placed before `text`. Second, there is no result for b2, so the call and result do not match. A failed call must also return a result.

steps.title: Step 4 Modification
steps.body: Include two `tool_result` in one user message first. In a1, set the schedule, and in b2, set `is_error` to true, and include information such as “Weather cannot be checked right now.” Description `text` is left behind.

steps.title: Step 5 Confirmation
steps.body: The model creates a response that provides the schedule and informs you that the weather is not available at this time. Because the results are grouped by ID, the schedule and weather are not reversed.

screens.outro: Now that I've finished editing, I'll close by summarizing the main points.

screens.title: Key takeaway: Results are returned grouped by request ID.
screens.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class. Check the answer to the question posed at the beginning, which is by what rule the results should be returned.

paragraphs: After answering the first question, the results are returned grouped by the request ID. We pair each call and result with `tool_use_id` for Claude and `call_id` for OpenAI and Gemini. Even if the order or number is correct, if the ids are different, the results will be reversed.

The results of calls received in parallel are all included in one next user message, and the `tool_result` block is placed before `text`. A call that failed to execute or failed must return a result showing `is_error` to be matched. The execution order is determined by the app. Independent read operations are executed in parallel, or sequentially if previous results are required or have side effects.
It is recommended that tool responses concisely return only high-signal information. You can save context by leaving out low-level identifiers and adding parameters that select the level of detail.

callout.label: rules to remember
callout.text: All results are grouped into one message by call ID, and tool_result is placed before text.

glossary.def: The model makes a request containing multiple tool calls in one response. The execution method is determined by the app.
A rule that pairs each call with its result by tool_use_id or call_id.
Tool failures are notified to the model with indicators and guidance text such as is_error.
It is a tool response method that succinctly returns only the necessary information, excluding low-level identifiers.

misconceptions.myth: If it is a parallel call, the results can be returned separately.
misconceptions.fact: All results must be put together in one user message and matched by ID.

misconceptions.myth: Parallel calls are always fast and safe.
misconceptions.fact: Calls that have side effects or depend on ordering are better done sequentially. Parallel is suitable for independent read operations.

misconceptions.myth: It is a good idea for tools to return as much information as possible.
misconceptions.fact: Unnecessary identifiers and long responses waste context. Please return only high signal information.

misconceptions.myth: You can write the explanatory sentence first and add the results afterwards.
misconceptions.fact: tool_result must come before text in the same user message. This order is a requirement of the API request format, and failure to do so will result in a 400 error.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The results are returned bundled with the request ID.
Independent read calls are executed in parallel, or sequentially if there are ordering or side effects.
It stores all results in one message and even flags failed calls as errors.
Tool responses concisely design only high-signal information.

closing.reflection: Does my tool's response contain only the information the model needs?

checks.q: There are two tool_use blocks with ids a1 and b2 in one response. What is the correct way to return a result?
options: Two tool_results are included in one user message, each with a tool_use_id, before the text.
Send only the first result first and wait for the model to request the rest for the rest.
Shuffle them in order of arrival and omit the ID.
Only successful results are sent and failed calls are omitted.
checks.explain: Put all tool_results together in one message and match them by tool_use_id. Failed calls should also return an error message to be matched.

wrong.1: Missing results cause the model to wait for mismatched calls.
wrong.2: Match by ID to prevent schedules and weather from changing.
wrong.3: An error result must also be returned for failed calls.
